paragraphs.heading: What an ice age is
paragraphs.text: An ice age is a stretch of time when Earth's surface and air are colder, so glaciers and polar ice caps last a long time or spread. People use the name both for very long cooling periods and for fairly short ones. Within one ice age, temperature and the amount of ice can swing back and forth. The colder spells are called glacials, and the relatively warmer ones are called interglacials.

paragraphs.heading: Icehouse and greenhouse
paragraphs.text: Over its history Earth switches between icehouse periods, when it has glaciers, and greenhouse periods, when it does not. For most of that history it has been in a greenhouse state with little or no permanent ice. Right now, though, it is in an icehouse called the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, which began 34 million years ago. The term ice age is also used for the Quaternary glaciation, which began 2.58 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: The most recent swings
paragraphs.text: The Last Interglacial ended 115,000 years ago. The Last Glacial Period came next, and its harshest stretch, the Last Glacial Maximum, peaked between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. The most recent glaciation was the Younger Dryas, from 12,800 to 11,700 years ago. Then the present warm interval, the Holocene, began 11,700 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from stray boulders
paragraphs.text: In 1742 the Geneva engineer and geographer Pierre Martel visited the Chamonix valley in the Alps. In his account two years later, he wrote that locals blamed the scattered erratic boulders on glaciers that had once reached much farther. In 1815 a carpenter and chamois hunter, Jean-Pierre Perraudin, gave the same explanation for boulders in the Val de Bagnes in Switzerland. Similar views turned up far away too: in the Chilean Andes in 1849–1850, local people told the naturalist Ernst von Bibra that old moraines were the work of glaciers.

paragraphs.heading: Scholars take up the idea
paragraphs.text: European scholars, meanwhile, wondered how the erratic material had been spread around, and from the mid-18th century some saw ice as the carrier. In 1742 the Swedish mining expert Daniel Tilas became the first to propose drifting sea ice as the reason for erratic boulders in Scandinavia and the Baltic. In 1795 James Hutton explained Alpine boulders by glacier action, and in 1818 Göran Wahlenberg described a glaciation of the Scandinavian peninsula, which he saw as a regional event. The geologist Jens Esmark went further and argued for a series of worldwide ice ages. In an 1824 paper he blamed changes in climate and tried to trace them to changes in Earth's orbit.

paragraphs.heading: A dam bursts
paragraphs.text: In 1815 Perraudin tried to win over the geologist Jean de Charpentier, pointing to deep scratches in the rock and giant boulders. Charpentier believed vast floods had left these marks and dismissed the idea as absurd. In 1818 the engineer Ignatz Venetz joined them to inspect a lake held back by an ice dam above the valley. When the dam broke it left only minor boulders and no scratches, so Venetz decided that only ice could explain the bigger signs. Charpentier, converted as well, published Venetz's paper with his own in 1834.

paragraphs.heading: Times of frozen water
paragraphs.text: Around the same time the German botanist Karl Friedrich Schimper was studying mosses on erratic boulders in the Bavarian uplands, and he began to ask where the stones had come from. After trips into the Bavarian Alps in the summer of 1835, he concluded that ice had carried them. He then proposed that the whole world had passed through cold periods of frozen water, which he called Verödungszeiten, or times of obliteration.
